rows.evidence: Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.2469/faj.v58.n4.2453: 'The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios', Lo, Andrew W., Financial Analysts Journal 58(4) 36-52, issued 2002-07, matching the registry. Publisher abstract (OpenAlex record for the DOI): 'I derive explicit expressions for the statistical distribution of the Sharpe ratio ... independently and identically distributed returns, stationary returns, and with time aggregation. I show that monthly Sharpe ratios cannot be annualized by multiplying by sqrt(12) except under very special circumstances ... the annual Sharpe ratio for a hedge fund can be overstated by as much as 65 percent because of the presence of serial correlation'. The claim (locator 'Abstract') says exactly this, and 'can overstate ... substantially' stays within the abstract's hedge-fund example. It is a journal article, not a working paper.

Crossref 10.1057/palgrave.jam.2250084: 'Comparing Sharpe ratios: So where are the p-values?', Opdyke, John Douglas, Journal of Asset Management 8(5) 308-336, 2007, matching the registry. Abstract (RePEc IDEAS page ideas.repec.org/a/pal/assmgt/v8y2007i5d10.1057_palgrave.jam.2250084.html): earlier usable derivations 'relied on the restrictive ... assumption of normally distributed returns'; the paper 'presents an easily implemented formula for the asymptotic distribution that is valid under ... stationary and ergodic returns — thus permitting time-varying conditional volatilities, serial correlation'. The claim wording matches the abstract. The full text is paywalled (Springer returned a JS challenge and SSRN 886728 returned 403), so only abstract-level attribution was checked. The contested scope is graded in L07-grade-opdyke2007.

Crossref 10.21314/jor.2012.255: 'The Sharpe ratio efficient frontier', Bailey, David; López de Prado, Marcos, Journal of Risk 15(2) 3-44, 2012-12, matching the registry. Open copy davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/sharpe-frontier.pdf (SSRN 1821643 version): Eq. (11) PSR(SR*) = Z[(SR^-SR*)sqrt(n-1)/sqrt(1-g3 SR^+(g4-1)/4 SR^2)] is formula (2) of the page. Eq. (8) uses g4 = E[(r-mu)^4]/sigma^4 (raw kurtosis), and Sec. 2.5 says 'n-1 is due to Bessel's correction'. This title-level reference has no locator.

Metadata: Crossref 10.3905/jpm.2014.40.5.094 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality', Bailey, David H.; López de Prado, Marcos, JPM 40(5) 94-107, 2014, matching the registry. Formula: open copy davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/deflated-sharpe.pdf (version of 31 Jul 2014, SSRN 2460551) p. 8 Eq. (2) has DSR = PSR(SR0) with sqrt(T-1) and (g4-1)/4, and SR0 = sqrt(V[{SR_n}])((1-g)Z^-1[1-1/N] + g Z^-1[1-(1/N)e^-1]). That is the page's (3); the normal case is g3 = 0, g4 = 3 (p. 10). Attribution defect: the paper defines N as 'the number of independent trials' (p. 8, below Eq. 2). Appendix A.3 (p. 14) says 'the N used to compute E[max{SR_n}] corresponds to the number of independent trials ... using M instead of N will overstate E[max{SR_n}]' and proposes N^ = rho^ + (1-rho^)M (Eq. 9), used with V[{SR_n}], 'the variance across the trials' estimated SR'. Definition 3.1 of the page instead sets N to the count of all trials and attributes the statistic to BLdP without noting the change. Section 4, Proposition 4.2 and Misconception 3 then label the source's own recipe a double count without naming the source. The page's mathematics is right: my script prop42_check.py Part C shows that BLdP's N^ paired with the cross-sectional variance understates the true hurdle by 2.2%, 9.1% and 23.5% at rho = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 (M = 100). But the reader is not told that the cited paper prescribes the opposite.
rows.fix: In Definition 3.1, state that Bailey & López de Prado (2014) define N as the number of independent trials. State that for correlated trials they propose the implied count N^ = rho^ + (1 - rho^)M, paired with the cross-sectional variance (appendix 'Estimating the number of independent trials'; check the appendix numbering in the JPM version before using it as a locator). Then say that this lesson, like the A8 contract, uses raw N with the cross-sectional variance, and that Proposition 4.2 shows the source's pairing double-counts correlation under equicorrelation. Repeat that pointer in Section 4 and in Misconception 3.

rows.evidence: Graded T. My grade is T: the result is proved on the page in full (see L07-math-thm1.2).
Graded T. My grade is T: substituting g3 = 0, g4 = 3 into (1) gives 1 + SR^2/2.

Graded B. My grade is B. The content is an asymptotic derivation published in the flagship peer-reviewed practitioner journal and later re-derived in generalized form: BLdP 2012 Sec. 2.4 lists Mertens 2002, Christie 2005 and Opdyke 2007. I found no published counter-evidence to Lo's results. T is not available because the locator is 'Abstract' and gives no equation-level proof locator.

Graded B. My grade is C. First, the Journal of Asset Management is not a top peer-reviewed venue (BLUEPRINT §3). Second, the claim's generality ('allowing ... serial correlation') is contested and the page gives one side only. The page's own PSR source, BLdP 2012 (davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/sharpe-frontier.pdf (SSRN 1821643 version), Sec. 2.4, p. 8), reports that 'Opdyke (2007) proved that the expressions in Mertens (2002) and Christie (2005) are in fact identical', so Mertens' expression, which is formula (1) of this page, 'appears to be valid under ... stationary and ergodic returns, and not only IID'. On that basis it claims PSR holds beyond IID (Sec. 1, p. 3). This conflicts with Lo (2002), whose stationary-case variance depends on autocorrelations, and with the page's own Section 5 and Section 6, which say formula (1) needs independence. My simulation (thm12_check.py: AR(1), phi = 0.3, SR = 0.1, T = 2000, 20,000 reps) gives T*Var(SR^) = 1.909 against formula (1)'s 1.005, so (1) with ordinary moments fails under serial correlation. Section 6 lists Opdyke among the results that 'relax' independence without telling the reader that the cited PSR paper reads his result as validating (1) itself.
rows.fix: Change data-grade to C. Rewrite to say that Opdyke states his formula is valid for stationary-ergodic returns, and that BLdP (2012, Sec. 2.4) read it as extending formula (1) beyond iid. Then say that for serially correlated returns the variance depends on the autocorrelations (Lo 2002), with a short lab or problem showing the AR(1) failure. If Opdyke's full text shows his formula uses long-run moments, say so with a page locator. Otherwise drop Opdyke from Section 6's list of results that relax independence.

rows.evidence: Checked the standard-error formula sqrt((1 - g3 SR + (g4-1)/4 SR^2)/(T-1)) and the g4 convention against the sources. BLdP 2012 Eq. (8) (davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/sharpe-frontier.pdf (SSRN 1821643 version) p. 8) gives Var = (1 + SR^2/2 - g3 SR + (g4-3)/4 SR^2)/n with g4 = E[(r-mu)^4]/sigma^4. That is algebraically equal to (1 - g3 SR + (g4-1)/4 SR^2)/n, and Sec. 2.5 uses n-1. BLdP 2014 Eq. (2) is the same, with normal g4 = 3 (p. 10). notation.json registers g4 as kurtosis 'not excess ... 3 under normality', and the A8 contract (Conventions table: Skewness and Kurtosis rows; sharpe_ratio_std) matches. Mertens (2002) is not in the registry. His form was checked through BLdP 2012's restatement, and Lo (2002)'s normal-iid case 1 + SR^2/2 is Corollary 1.3.

Re-derived. Step 1: Cov(r-mu, (r-mu)^2) = mu3 and Var((r-mu)^2) = mu4 - sigma^4. Step 2: the identity s^2 = T/(T-1)(mean((r-mu)^2) - (rbar-mu)^2) holds, and sqrt(T)(rbar-mu)^2 -> 0 in probability. Step 3: the gradient of m/sqrt(v) is (1/sigma, -mu/(2 sigma^3)), and the quadratic form is 1 - SR g3 + SR^2 (g4-1)/4. Assumptions are complete: iid, E r^4 < inf, sigma > 0. Independent Monte Carlo (thm12_check.py: Gamma(4) shocks with g3 = -1, g4 = 4.5, T = 2000, 20,000 reps) gave T*Var(SR^) = 1.0500 vs 1.0522 at SR = 0.05, 1.2215 vs 1.2350 (+-0.0122) at 0.20, and 0.8818 vs 0.8697 (+-0.0088) at -0.15. All are within about 1.4 Monte Carlo standard errors.

Re-derived: PSR = Phi(z) = 1 - p, PSR(SR^) = Phi(0) = 1/2, and the argument of Phi is affine in SR* with slope -1/se, so PSR is strictly decreasing in SR*. Remark 2.4 correctly separates this from a posterior, whereas BLdP 2012 p. 9 call PSR a 'probability of skill'.

Checked the expected-maximum approximation with the Euler–Mascheroni constant. davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/deflated-sharpe.pdf (version of 31 Jul 2014, SSRN 2460551) p. 8 Eq. (2) gives (1-g)Z^-1[1-1/N] + g Z^-1[1-(1/N)e^-1], and the paper's Snippet 1 (p. 13) codes (1-emc)*ppf(1-1/N) + emc*ppf(1-1/(N*e)), which is the page's (3). The constant 0.5772156649015329 matches the notation.json \emgamma and the A8 contract. Recomputed brackets: N=2 0.5198, N=3 0.8528, N=10 1.5746, N=25 1.9971, N=40 2.1895, N=100 2.5306 (exact E[max] 2.5076, +0.92%), N=1000 3.2551. The convention for N is handled in L07-cite-bailey2014deflated.

This is the builder's own result. I re-derived it in full. (i) SR_n - mean(SR) = sqrt((1-rho)/T)(eps_n - mean(eps)), and E[sample variance of iid N(0,1)] = 1, so E[S^2] = (1-rho)/T. (ii) max_n SR_n = C + sqrt((1-rho)/T) max eps_n with E[C] = 0. The final sentence uses sqrt(E[S^2]), as stated. N >= 2 is implicit in the N-1 divisor. Simulation (prop42_check.py Part A, the proposition's own model, N = 100, T = 1260, 200,000 reps) at rho = 0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8: T*E[S^2] = 0.9996, 0.7999, 0.5001, 0.2000 (theory 1, 0.8, 0.5, 0.2); sqrt(T) E[max] = 2.5079, 2.2445, 1.7725, 1.1244 against 2.5076, 2.2429, 1.7731, 1.1214, all within 1.5 standard errors. Part B used Sharpe ratios estimated from equicorrelated returns (400 reps): rho = 0.2 gave 0.7983 and 2.218 +- 0.029, and rho = 0.8 gave 0.2006 and 1.159 +- 0.045. Both are consistent.

The solution says 'the spread of SR*_b - SR^ estimates the sampling distribution of SR^', so the null distribution of SR^ under SR = SR0 is SR0 + (SR*_b - SR^). It then defines the p-value as 'the share of SR^ - SR*_b + SR0 at or above SR^', which uses the reflected deviation. Algebraically that is the share of SR*_b <= SR0, the percentile-interval p-value, not the shift (basic-bootstrap) p-value its own rationale implies: the share of SR*_b >= 2 SR^ - SR0. The two coincide only when the bootstrap distribution is symmetric. They differ at second order under skewness, which is the setting of this lesson.
rows.fix: Replace the formula with 'the share of SR0 + (SR*_b - SR^) at or above SR^, i.e. of SR*_b >= 2 SR^ - SR0'. Alternatively keep the percentile version, call it that ('the share of SR*_b at or below SR0'), and justify it.

Re-derived: C(S, S/2) = (S/(S/2)) C(S-1, S/2-1) = 2 C(S-1, S/2-1), and complementation is a fixed-point-free involution. Counts computed for S = 4, 6, 8, 10, 16: 6, 20, 70, 252, 12870 and 3, 10, 35, 126, 6435.

This is the builder's own result. I re-derived it. Disjoint row sets with independent rows make n* independent of the OOS metric vector. Exchangeable columns with a.s. distinct metrics make each fixed column's OOS rank uniform on {1..N}, hence the rank of n* is uniform. lambda <= 0 iff r <= (N+1)/2, and floor((N+1)/2) of the N ranks qualify. Linearity over the dependent splits gives the result. Simulation (thm41_check.py: T = 240, S = 6, 3000 reps per case; page convention) for iid normal: N=2 0.5081 (+-0.006), N=3 0.6653, N=4 0.5091, N=5 0.5964, N=21 0.5201 against 0.5, 0.6667, 0.5, 0.6, 0.5238. A rerun with seed 99, S = 4 and 12,000 reps gave N=2 0.5010 +- 0.0034 and N=4 0.5002 +- 0.0028. An exchangeable common factor (rho = 0.8) gave N=3 0.6659 and N=4 0.5040. The result holds as stated. Its dependence on definitions and ties is in the next two rows.

'The next theorem gives it exactly, for any dependence between the configurations.' This is false: the theorem needs exchangeable columns. Counterexample: N = 3, where columns 1 and 2 are near-duplicates and column 3 is independent. By hand the null PBO is 1/2*1/2 + 1/2*3/4 = 0.625, and simulation gives 0.6253 +- 0.0059 (thm41_check.py), not the theorem's 2/3.
rows.fix: Replace with 'for any exchangeable dependence between the configurations (any common correlation)'.

rows.evidence: Builder flag: the theorem's value depends on the PBO definition. In simulation (thm41_check.py, iid normal), the mean PBO under each convention is as follows. Page (lambda <= 0): 0.508, 0.665, 0.509, 0.596, 0.520 for N = 2, 3, 4, 5, 21. Strict (lambda < 0): odd N gives (N-1)/(2N) (0.335, 0.396, 0.472). Source's formal Definition 2.2 (p. 10, Eq. 2.2: P[r < N/2]): 0.000, 0.335, 0.257, 0.396, 0.472, i.e. (ceil(N/2)-1)/N, which is 0.45 at N = 20. With ties (+-1 returns, T = 40, S = 4), the page convention gives 0.556 (N=2) and 0.542 (N=4); the theorem correctly excludes ties by assumption. The page says the non-strict inequality is 'the convention this module's project uses'. It never says that the cited paper's own Definition 2.2 uses r < N/2, which gives a different null value, or that the paper's estimator phi = int_-inf^0 f(lambda) d lambda leaves the atom at lambda = 0 ambiguous. A reader who implements the source's definition gets 0.45, not 0.5, for Lab 2's N = 20.
rows.fix: Add a remark after Theorem 4.1 covering three points. BBLdPZ's Definition 2.2 counts r < N/2, under which the exchangeable-null value is (ceil(N/2) - 1)/N. Their CSCV estimator integrates the logit density up to 0, so the convention at lambda = 0 decides odd N. Ties at the median (average ranks) put mass at lambda = 0 and raise the expected PBO above (3).

rows.evidence: 'A configuration can be a genuine, StepM-significant discovery with a high DSR and still come from a process with a high PBO: one real edge among thousands of tries ... That is exactly the state of Lab 3 at 200 trials.' I checked this in l08_numbers.py. In Lab 3 at 200 trials the genuine configuration's full-sample edge is 0.10*sqrt(1000) = 3.162. It is the full-sample winner with probability 0.651. It clears the one-sided Bonferroni 5% bound z = 3.481, an upper bound on the StepM critical value, with probability only 0.375. Its DSR at the true edge is Phi(3.162 - bracket(200) = 2.766) = 0.654. Lab 3's PBO at 200 trials is 0.34, below one half. There are 200 tries, not thousands. None of the four conditions holds typically.
rows.fix: Delete 'That is exactly the state of Lab 3 at 200 trials', or point instead to a scenario that has been checked (Problem R3, once corrected).

rows.evidence: 'A research log that omits failed configurations ... biases the PBO downward' has no claim span or key, and simulation contradicts it (l08_sims.py omit: 100 null configurations, T = 1000, S = 10, 80 reps). With all 100 logged the PBO is 0.5025 +- 0.018. Logging only the 20 best full-sample configurations, i.e. omitting the 80 failures, gives 0.8145 +- 0.019. Logging a random 20 gives 0.521. With one genuine configuration (SR 0.15), omitting the failures moves the PBO from 0.1345 to 0.2197. Omitting failures biased PBO upward, through the compensation effect the source itself describes (Sec. 3.2). The direction stated on the page follows the source's Sec. 5.2 ('Hiding trials will lead to an underestimation of the overfit'), which is not cited here.
rows.fix: Rewrite: an incomplete trial matrix changes what PBO measures, and the sign of the distortion depends on which trials are missing (omitting the weakest full-sample performers raised PBO from 0.50 to 0.81 in a pure-noise simulation). If the source's contrary statement is kept, mark it as a C claim citing bailey2016probability Sec. 5.2, with this counter-evidence (a lab or problem).

rows.evidence: The solution predicts 'about 0.55, barely above the null value' and concludes that 'CSCV will usually not flag this process'. Simulating the stated design (20 nulls plus a configuration at daily SR +0.2 then -0.2, 1000 days, S = 10) gave mean PBO 0.591 +- 0.015 (150 reps, seed 8080) and 0.610 +- 0.0125 (200 reps, seed 31337). 74% of single estimates were at or above 0.5 and only 5.5% below 0.3. The 0.55 approximation is off by about 4-5 standard errors. Under the page's own reading rule (Misconception 2: 'Evidence against it is a PBO near or above one half'; R1: approve only if PBO is well below one half), CSCV usually does flag this process. It cannot tell a dead regime from noise.
rows.fix: Correct the expected value to about 0.6, for example by counting that the dying configuration wins only about 76% of the k >= 4 splits and that N = 21 has a median rank. Rewrite the conclusion: 'CSCV returns a PBO near or above one half, the verdict it gives a pure-noise search; it says the selection is uninformative but cannot see that the selected strategy died, which walk-forward shows directly.'
